concepts.title: Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind
concepts.definition: Al-Biruni, born at Khwarizm in 973 and taken to Ghazni by Mahmud in 1017, learned Sanskrit to write the Kitab-ul-Hind, a survey of Indian religion, sciences and society written in Arabic; he named two barriers to understanding - language and religious self-centredness - and worked past them through Sanskrit texts.
concepts.key_idea: An outsider's method of careful textual comparison made the Kitab a benchmark of cross-cultural description.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehs201.txt Al-Biruni biography, Kitab-ul-Hind and barriers sections
question_patterns: who was Al-Biruni and when did he come to India
name the barriers he identified for understanding India
describe the structure of the Kitab-ul-Hind
why did Al-Biruni learn Sanskrit
what did he report about Indian religion and science
evaluate his account's reliability

solution_steps.explain: born 973 at Khwarizm, arriving with Mahmud's campaigns in 1017
language differences and religious self-centredness blocked understanding
reading Sanskrit texts first-hand let him describe beliefs in their own terms

concepts.title: Ibn Battuta's Rihla
concepts.definition: Ibn Battuta of Tangier, born in 1304, reached India in 1333 and served as qazi of Delhi under Muhammad bin Tughlaq; his Rihla describes cities, bazaars, the postal system of horse and foot runners, and Indian marvels, written on return to Morocco from memory and dictation.
concepts.key_idea: The Rihla prizes the surprising: communication systems, market abundance and administrative reach impressed a Moroccan accustomed to smaller scale.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehs201.txt Ibn Battuta biography, Rihla and postal system sections
question_patterns: who was Ibn Battuta and what office did he hold in Delhi
describe the postal system he praised
what surprised him about Indian bazaars and communications
how and where was the Rihla composed
compare his view of Delhi with Al-Biruni's approach
what does the Rihla reveal about the fourteenth century

solution_steps.explain: born 1304, arriving in Delhi in 1333 as qazi
horse and foot runners carried news swiftly across the sultanate
dictated from memory in Morocco, the Rihla mixes precision and wonder

concepts.title: Francois Bernier's Comparison
concepts.definition: Francois Bernier, a French physician who reached India in 1656 and served at the Mughal court, wrote Travels in the Mughal Empire comparing India with Europe; he saw absence of private property in land as the root of Mughal despotism and decline, a view later labelled the theory of Oriental despotism.
concepts.key_idea: Bernier's comparisons told as much about European anxieties as about India: his letters shaped Enlightenment debates on property and empire.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehs201.txt Bernier biography, property theory and comparisons sections
question_patterns: who was Bernier and when did he write
state his theory about land ownership in the Mughal empire
what is Oriental despotism and its later career
how did Bernier compare Mughal cities with European ones
criticise Bernier's account of artisans and manufacturing
relate his views to European political debates

solution_steps.explain: reached India by 1656, serving at the Mughal court
crown ownership of land, he claimed, bred despotism and poverty
modern historians find his picture exaggerated though revealing

concepts.title: Women, Slavery and Social Practice in Travellers' Accounts
concepts.definition: Travellers recorded social practices from their own angles: Bernier and others described sati and slavery, Ibn Battuta noted slave markets and women's work in cities, and all accounts need reading against their authors' purposes and audiences.
concepts.key_idea: Travellers' notes on women and slavery show real practices filtered through moral judgements and travel-writing conventions.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehs201.txt sati, slavery and women's labour descriptions
question_patterns: how did travellers describe sati and with what judgements
what does Ibn Battuta report about slavery
describe women's work recorded by travellers
why must travellers' accounts be used critically
compare travellers' views of caste and social division
what purposes shaped what travellers chose to record

solution_steps.explain: sati, slave markets and women's weaving appear in the accounts
authors wrote for home audiences with moral agendas
cross-checking travellers against local sources restores balance

concepts.title: Travellers' Timeline
concepts.definition: The three travellers span five centuries: Al-Biruni came in 1017 aged forty-four, Ibn Battuta in 1333 aged twenty-nine, and Bernier by 1656; the differences are found by subtracting each birth year from the year of arrival.
concepts.key_idea: Each traveller's age at arrival equals the arrival year minus the birth year.
question_patterns: compute Al-Biruni's age when he reached India
compute Ibn Battuta's age at his Indian arrival
arrange the travellers in chronological order
how many centuries separate the first and last accounts
what changed between the eleventh and seventeenth centuries
why do dates matter for reading travellers

solution_steps.explain: Al-Biruni born 973, arrived 1017; Ibn Battuta born 1304, arrived 1333
the difference gives the age at arrival

worked_examples.question_pattern: Al-Biruni was born in 973 and reached India in 1017. Compute his age at arrival.
Describe the postal system of the Delhi sultanate as Ibn Battuta saw it.

solution_template.explain: the uluq used horses at stages, the dawa used foot runners
news and fruit travelled far faster than ordinary traffic
communication reach impressed him more than monuments

worked_examples.question_pattern: State Bernier's land ownership thesis and one modern criticism of it.

solution_template.explain: crown ownership of land left peasants without incentive, breeding despotism
records show layered property rights and thriving rural exchange, contradicting stagnation
his account reveals European debates as much as Indian realities
